findings.title: Public rank priced by display and outcome
findings.claim: Across 19:73–76, the boast ranks the two parties by station and council; 19:74 carries that comparative into earlier cohorts’ furnishings and outward appearance, while 19:75–76 answer public rank with a verdict about support and a distinct measure of what endures and returns.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries the comparative أَحْسَنُ through أَثَاثًا وَرِءْيًا. The independent trigger is 19:73’s comparison of خَيْرٌ مَقَامًا and أَحْسَنُ نَدِيًّا; 19:75 then names a worse station and weaker host for the present disputants, and 19:76 calls enduring deeds better in reward and return. These contacts move the reading from a display-based scorecard toward outcomes that display cannot secure.
findings.reader_payoff: The comparison is answered on terms its audience can recognize: furnishings, visible appearance, venue, and public company count as rank markers, but they do not guarantee backing or lasting return.
findings.containment: The weak host in 19:75 concerns the present disputants, not the destroyed cohort of 19:74. The righteous deeds and their recompense in 19:76 are a separate standard, not a lexical meaning of furnishings or appearance in 19:74.

findings.claim: The focus’s earlier qarn occupies one position in a sequence: 19:59 explicitly places successors after predecessors, while 19:63 speaks of inheritance from the servants who receive the promised Garden. Their contact makes the focus’s destruction part of a succession horizon instead of a static example of an affluent group’s fall.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees historical turnover around the cohort, while the pericope’s promised inheritance points to a different source of lasting possession.
findings.containment: The Garden in 19:63 is inherited by the pious; the ayah does not say that the destroyed cohort’s furniture or status passes to its successors. The inheritance contact is a bounded transfer parallel, not an identification of the two inheritances.
